# Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, First Part

**Theorem.** Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$, where $a<b$. Let $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by
$$F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt .$$
Then $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$: that is, $F$ is differentiable at every point $x\in[a,b]$ (one-sidedly at the endpoints) and $F'(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in[a,b]$.

(If $a=b$, the interval $[a,b]=\{a\}$ is a single point, at which no difference quotient can be formed; the statement is then vacuous. So $a<b$ is assumed throughout.)

## 0. Conventions and standing facts

$\int_c^d g$ denotes the Riemann integral, which we use in its Darboux formulation: for a bounded $g$ on $[c,d]$ ($c<d$) and a partition $P:\;c=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=d$ put
$$L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n \Bigl(\inf_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g\Bigr)(t_i-t_{i-1}),\qquad U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n \Bigl(\sup_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g\Bigr)(t_i-t_{i-1}),$$
and $g$ is integrable with integral $I$ iff $\sup_P L(g,P)=\inf_P U(g,P)=I$. (This is equivalent to the Riemann-sum definition; we use only the displayed characterisation.)

We adopt the usual orientation convention
$$\int_d^c g(t)\,dt := -\int_c^d g(t)\,dt\quad(c<d),\qquad \int_c^c g(t)\,dt := 0 .$$

**Derivative on a closed interval.** For $x\in[a,b]$ set
$$H_x:=\{h\in\mathbb{R}:\ h\neq 0,\ x+h\in[a,b]\}.$$
Since $a<b$, the number $0$ is an accumulation point of $H_x$ for every $x\in[a,b]$: if $x<b$ then $(0,\,b-x]\subseteq H_x$, and if $x>a$ then $[a-x,\,0)\subseteq H_x$, and at least one of these holds. We say that $F$ is *differentiable at $x$ with derivative $L$*, written $F'(x)=L$, if
$$\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\in H_x}}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=L ,$$
i.e. if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\bigl|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-L\bigr|<\varepsilon$ for all $h\in H_x$ with $0<|h|<\delta$. For $x\in(a,b)$ this is the ordinary two-sided derivative; at $x=a$ it is the right-hand derivative and at $x=b$ the left-hand derivative. A *primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$* is a function $F$ on $[a,b]$ which is differentiable in this sense at every point of $[a,b]$ and satisfies $F'(x)=f(x)$ there.

We take as known the following two standard facts about the integral.

**(I1) (Continuous $\Rightarrow$ integrable.)** If $g$ is continuous on a closed bounded interval $[c,d]$ with $c<d$, then $g$ is (Riemann–Darboux) integrable on $[c,d]$.

**(I2) (Additivity over subintervals.)** If $g$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and $c\le e\le d$, then $g$ is integrable on $[c,e]$ and on $[e,d]$, and
$$\int_c^d g=\int_c^e g+\int_e^d g$$
(with the convention $\int_c^c g=0$ covering the degenerate cases $e=c$ and $e=d$).

We also use the **Extreme Value Theorem** (a continuous real function on a closed bounded interval attains a minimum and a maximum) and the **Intermediate Value Theorem**.

**(I3) Lemma (Bounds).** *Let $g$ be integrable on $[c,d]$ with $c<d$, and suppose $m\le g(t)\le M$ for all $t\in[c,d]$. Then*
$$m(d-c)\ \le\ \int_c^d g\ \le\ M(d-c).$$

*Proof.* Let $P:\;c=t_0<\dots<t_n=d$ be **any** partition. For each $i$ we have $m\le\inf_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g$ and $\sup_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g\le M$, since $m$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound for $g$ on the subinterval. As $t_i-t_{i-1}>0$,
$$L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl(\inf_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g\Bigr)(t_i-t_{i-1})\ \ge\ \sum_{i=1}^n m\,(t_i-t_{i-1})=m(d-c),$$
and likewise $U(g,P)\le M(d-c)$. Hence $m(d-c)$ is a lower bound for the set $\{L(g,P):P\}$ and $M(d-c)$ an upper bound for $\{U(g,P):P\}$. Taking any single partition $P_0$ (say the trivial one $c<d$) and using integrability,
$$\int_c^d g=\sup_P L(g,P)\ \ge\ L(g,P_0)\ \ge\ m(d-c),\qquad \int_c^d g=\inf_P U(g,P)\ \le\ U(g,P_0)\ \le\ M(d-c).$$
$\blacksquare$

*Note.* The proof uses only the inequalities $L(g,P)\ge m(d-c)$ and $U(g,P)\le M(d-c)$, valid for **every** partition, together with $\int g=\sup_P L=\inf_P U$. It nowhere asserts that $L(g,P)$, $U(g,P)$ and $\int_c^d g$ coincide for some particular partition $P$ — which is false in general (e.g. $g(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ with $P:0<1$ gives $L=0$, $U=1$, $\int=\tfrac12$).

## 1. $F$ is well defined

Let $x\in[a,b]$. If $x=a$, then $F(a)=\int_a^a f=0$ by convention. If $x>a$, then $[a,x]\subseteq[a,b]$, and the restriction of $f$ to $[a,x]$ is continuous (a restriction of a continuous function to a subinterval is continuous). By **(I1)**, $f$ is integrable on $[a,x]$, so $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is a well-defined real number. Thus $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is well defined. Likewise $f$ is integrable on every closed subinterval $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$ with $c<d$.

## 2. A Mean Value Theorem for integrals

**Lemma.** *Let $g$ be continuous on $[c,d]$ with $c<d$. Then there exists $\xi\in[c,d]$ such that*
$$\int_c^d g(t)\,dt=g(\xi)\,(d-c).$$

*Proof.* By **(I1)**, $g$ is integrable on $[c,d]$. By the Extreme Value Theorem there are $p,q\in[c,d]$ with
$$m:=g(p)=\min_{t\in[c,d]}g(t),\qquad M:=g(q)=\max_{t\in[c,d]}g(t),$$
so that $m\le g(t)\le M$ for all $t\in[c,d]$. By Lemma **(I3)**,
$$m(d-c)\le\int_c^d g\le M(d-c).$$
Since $d-c>0$ we may divide by it, obtaining
$$m\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ M,\qquad\text{where }\ \mu:=\frac{1}{d-c}\int_c^d g .$$

*Case $m=M$.* Then $g(t)=m$ for all $t\in[c,d]$, and $\mu=m=g(c)$; take $\xi:=c\in[c,d]$.

*Case $m<M$.* Then $p\neq q$. Let $J:=[\min(p,q),\max(p,q)]$, a nondegenerate closed interval with $J\subseteq[c,d]$. The function $g$ is continuous on $J$, and $\mu$ lies between the values $g(p)=m$ and $g(q)=M$ attained by $g$ at the two endpoints of $J$. By the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists $\xi\in J\subseteq[c,d]$ with $g(\xi)=\mu$.

In either case $\xi\in[c,d]$ and $g(\xi)=\mu$; multiplying by $d-c$ gives $\int_c^d g=g(\xi)(d-c)$. $\blacksquare$

(We only claim $\xi\in[c,d]$; the sharper statement $\xi\in(c,d)$ is true but is not needed here.)

## 3. The increment of $F$

**Claim.** *For every $x\in[a,b]$ and every $h\in H_x$,*
$$F(x+h)-F(x)=\int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt,$$
*with the orientation convention of §0.*

*Proof.* Note first that $x,x+h\in[a,b]$, so all integrals below are over subintervals of $[a,b]$ and exist by §1.

*Case $h>0$.* Then $a\le x<x+h\le b$. Apply **(I2)** to $f$ on $[a,x+h]$ with intermediate point $x$ (legitimate since $a\le x\le x+h$):
$$\int_a^{x+h}f=\int_a^x f+\int_x^{x+h}f,$$
i.e. $F(x+h)=F(x)+\int_x^{x+h}f$, which is the claim. (If $x=a$, both sides read $F(a+h)=0+\int_a^{a+h}f$.)

*Case $h<0$.* Then $a\le x+h<x\le b$. Apply **(I2)** to $f$ on $[a,x]$ with intermediate point $x+h$ (legitimate since $a\le x+h\le x$):
$$\int_a^{x}f=\int_a^{x+h}f+\int_{x+h}^{x}f,$$
i.e. $F(x)-F(x+h)=\int_{x+h}^x f$. By the orientation convention $\int_x^{x+h}f=-\int_{x+h}^x f$, hence
$$F(x+h)-F(x)=-\int_{x+h}^x f=\int_x^{x+h}f . \qquad\blacksquare$$

## 4. The difference quotient equals a value of $f$

**Claim.** *For every $x\in[a,b]$ and every $h\in H_x$ there is a point $\xi_h$ in the closed interval with endpoints $x$ and $x+h$ such that*
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(\xi_h).$$
*In particular $\xi_h\in[a,b]$ and $|\xi_h-x|\le|h|$.*

*Proof.* Let $h\in H_x$.

*Case $h>0$.* Set $c:=x$, $d:=x+h$; then $c<d$, $d-c=h$ and $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$. As $f$ is continuous on $[c,d]$, the Lemma of §2 yields $\xi_h\in[x,x+h]$ with
$$\int_x^{x+h}f=f(\xi_h)\,h .$$
Combining with §3 and dividing by $h\neq0$:
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}f=f(\xi_h).$$

*Case $h<0$.* Set $c:=x+h$, $d:=x$; then $c<d$, $d-c=-h>0$ and $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$. The Lemma of §2 yields $\xi_h\in[x+h,x]$ with
$$\int_{x+h}^{x}f=f(\xi_h)\,(-h).$$
By §3,
$$F(x+h)-F(x)=\int_x^{x+h}f=-\int_{x+h}^{x}f=-f(\xi_h)(-h)=f(\xi_h)\,h .$$
Dividing by $h\neq0$ gives $\dfrac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(\xi_h)$.

In both cases $\xi_h$ lies in the closed interval with endpoints $x$ and $x+h$; that interval has length $|h|$ and contains $x$, so $|\xi_h-x|\le|h|$, and it is contained in $[a,b]$. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Passage to the limit

Fix $x\in[a,b]$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $f$ is continuous at $x$ (as a function on $[a,b]$), there exists $\delta>0$ such that
$$t\in[a,b]\ \text{ and }\ |t-x|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon .$$
Let $h\in H_x$ with $0<|h|<\delta$. By §4 there is $\xi_h\in[a,b]$ with $|\xi_h-x|\le|h|<\delta$ and $\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(\xi_h)$. Therefore
$$\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|=\bigl|f(\xi_h)-f(x)\bigr|<\varepsilon .$$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, and $0$ is an accumulation point of $H_x$ (§0), so that the limit is meaningful, we conclude
$$\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\in H_x}}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(x),$$
that is, $F$ is differentiable at $x$ with $F'(x)=f(x)$.

As $x\in[a,b]$ was arbitrary, $F$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ (one-sidedly at $a$ and at $b$) and $F'=f$ on $[a,b]$. By definition, $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$. $\blacksquare$

## Remarks

1. **An alternative to §2.** The Mean Value Theorem for integrals can be avoided. With $\delta$ as in §5 and $h\in H_x$, $0<|h|<\delta$, the function $t\mapsto f(t)-f(x)$ is continuous, hence integrable, on the interval with endpoints $x$ and $x+h$, and satisfies $-\varepsilon\le f(t)-f(x)\le\varepsilon$ there (its points are within $|h|<\delta$ of $x$). Lemma **(I3)** and linearity of the *integral* (a standard property; note that lower Darboux sums themselves are **not** linear, which is why the argument is run at the level of the integral) give
$$\bigl|F(x+h)-F(x)-f(x)h\bigr|=\Bigl|\int_x^{x+h}\bigl(f(t)-f(x)\bigr)\,dt\Bigr|\le\varepsilon|h| ,$$
(the orientation convention handling $h<0$), whence the same conclusion after dividing by $|h|$.

2. **Continuity of $f$ is essential**, not merely convenient: for $f=\chi_{[0,\infty)}$ on $[-1,1]$ (integrable, discontinuous at $0$) one gets $F(x)=\max(x,0)$, which is not differentiable at $0$. The theorem's conclusion $F'=f$ everywhere therefore genuinely uses continuity at each point, as in §5.

3. Since $F$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, it is in particular continuous on $[a,b]$. (The implication runs this way only; continuity alone would not give differentiability.)
